Open Mind · open research, started November 2026

Every theory of consciousness is still unproven, so we test them all and build a better one

Goal: find the most accurate theory of human consciousness, by 2027. Today's theories may all be wrong. We test each one's riskiest predictions on open brain recordings, list every hard fact a true theory must explain, and build our own theory where the existing ones fail. Every result is published, failures included.

Take a taskRead the findings

01The problem

Nobody can yet say which brain activity makes an experience

Here “consciousness” means experience: there is something it is like to be you right now. Researchers ask two questions about it: whether someone is conscious at all, and what they are conscious of.

The usual method flashes the same picture many times. Sometimes people see it and sometimes they miss it. Whatever differs in the brain between the two is a candidate for the activity behind experience.

Many theories explain those differences, and they disagree about where in the brain experience happens. In 2025 the largest head-to-head test so far, COGITATE, pitted two of them against each other. Neither won.

What scientists agree on, and what they don't

02Where we are

The field can tell awake from deep sleep, but no theory has won a fair test

Five levels of claim, so that partial progress has a precise meaning. The best measure so far needs a magnetic pulse and special equipment, and the top step is empty.

Track our progress

03Found so far

Open data can test dreaming, but not brain-injured patients or ketamine

So far these are measurements of the ground we stand on, not tests of a theory. The first sealed tests are running. Each result appears here once it lands, whichever way it goes.

  • About 2,400 open test cases where sleep and experience can disagree, all from sleep

    We labelled every recording in the open datasets by what tells us the person's experience. 2,417 are awakenings from sleep followed by a report of experience or no experience. None comes from anaesthesia.

  • The ketamine evidence is one small group of people

    Three well-known papers show that measures follow experience under ketamine. All three use the same volunteers, so they count as one result, not three.

  • Splitting by time slices instead of by person fakes a result

    We built fake data with no real effect. Training and testing on slices from the same people made it look strong. Splitting by person made it look like chance, as it should.

All 5 findings, with their evidence

04How we test

A result counts only if it was sealed first and survives an attempt to break it

Anyone can find a pattern by trying analyses until one works. So each test is written down and fingerprinted before the data are opened, run on people the method never saw, and handed to someone else to break.

The rules, and what counts as done

05Open data

Reports given on waking are open only for sleep

We checked every open dataset against one question: what tells us whether the person was experiencing anything? The best answer is what they said when woken. 2,417 awakenings from sleep have such a report, all in the DREAM database.

No open recordings from brain-injured patients exist, and none from people who were unresponsive on ketamine but reported dreams afterwards. These are the gaps that most limit what anyone can test.

Download the counts

06Help

The fastest help is an AI agent taking an open task

Point a strong AI agent at a task on our board, with the rules and the brief. Or bring data: these would raise our odds most.

  • An open TMS-EEG dataset covering sleep, anaesthesia and patients, so the perturbational complexity index can be tested directly.
  • Open, pooled dream reports from serial-awakening studies.
  • COGITATE experiment 2 or INTREPID data released after we seal our predictions, which would give a clean prospective test.
